doc_title: Annual Report of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

structure.title: About the Federal Reserve
structure.summary:
iii
About the Federal Reserve
The Federal Reserve was created by an act of Congress on December 23, 1913, to provide the nation with a safer, more flexible, and more stable monetary and financial system. In establishing the Federal Reserve System, the United States was divided geographically into 12 Districts, each with a separately incorporated Reserve Bank.
For more information about the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve System, visit the Board’s website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/default.htm. Online versions of the Board’s annual report are available at https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/annual- report/default.htm.

structure.title: 1 Overview
structure.summary: The 2023 Annual Report describes the Federal Reserve’s operations across monetary policy, financial stability, supervision and regulation, payment systems, and consumer protection and community development. It also explains the System’s structure of 12 Reserve Banks and a seven-member Board of Governors, and directs readers to appendixes containing leadership information, FOMC minutes, financial audits and oversight reviews, budgets and currency costs, policy actions, litigation, and historical operational statistics.

structure.title: 2 Monetary Policy and Economic Developments

nodes.title: March 2024 Summary
Recent Economic and Financial Developments
nodes.summary: The report reviews recent U.S. and international economic and financial conditions. U.S. inflation has fallen considerably but remains above target, labor markets are tight though more balanced, GDP growth was strong in 2023, and business investment and manufacturing softened. Financial conditions tightened after further FOMC rate increases, while credit became more costly and bank lending slowed. The banking system remained resilient, but elevated asset valuations, leverage, asset-value losses, and rising funding costs posed risks. Foreign growth and inflation weakened, foreign central banks paused tightening, and some began easing. The FOMC maintained its 5.25–5.50 percent policy-rate range and required greater evidence of sustainably declining inflation before reducing rates.

nodes.title: Monetary Policy
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial stability, international economic and inflation developments, and U.S. monetary policy. It describes a resilient banking system alongside elevated asset valuations, leverage, funding-cost, and fixed-rate-asset risks; weaker foreign growth, declining but uneven inflation, paused or easing central-bank policies, and a slight rise in the dollar. It explains that the FOMC has held the federal funds rate at 5.25–5.50 percent and will await stronger evidence of sustained 2 percent inflation before cutting, while continuing a gradual balance-sheet reduction that has removed about $1.4 trillion in securities since runoff began. A related chart presents Treasury and policy rates from 2008 to February 2024. The text also notes that tight labor-market conditions narrowed employment and wage disparities among demographic and educational groups, with some gaps reaching historical lows in 2023, though inequalities remained.

nodes.title: Special Topics
nodes.summary: The text reviews interest-rate developments and Federal Reserve policy. It describes Treasury yields and the federal funds target through February 2024, the Fed's data-dependent approach to rate adjustments, and its ongoing balance-sheet reduction, including the scale of runoff and plans to preserve an ample-reserves regime. It also covers narrowing but persistent employment and earnings disparities, the effects of higher mortgage rates and supply constraints on housing, developments in the Fed's balance sheet and money markets, and the reduced policy-rate prescriptions of simple monetary policy rules as inflation and labor-market imbalances improved.

This section reviews the Federal Reserve's March 2024 assessment of monetary policy and economic developments, including easing but still-elevated inflation, strong output and employment, tighter financial conditions, and weakening business and manufacturing activity. It examines resilient yet vulnerable banking and financial markets, softer foreign growth and inflation, and the FOMC's continued 5.25–5.50 percent policy rate and balance-sheet runoff pending sustained progress toward 2 percent inflation. It also covers interest-rate data, ample-reserves policy, housing and money-market conditions, financial stability, narrowing but persistent employment and earnings disparities, and the implications of monetary policy rules.

nodes.title: June 2023 Summary
Recent Economic and Financial Developments
nodes.summary: The June 2023 assessment describes inflation that has eased but remains significantly above 2 percent, a very tight but gradually cooling labor market, and modest economic growth amid tighter financial conditions. The FOMC raised rates to 5–5¼ percent and continued balance-sheet reduction, while signaling a slower, data-dependent approach to further tightening. The report reviews easing goods and housing inflation, persistent services inflation, resilient but slowing consumer and business activity, weak housing, tightening credit, and mixed corporate-finance conditions. It finds the banking system broadly resilient despite three bank failures and notes elevated real-estate valuations, debt and nonbank-finance vulnerabilities. International activity rebounded but inflation remained elevated abroad, prompting continued foreign monetary tightening. The Federal Reserve stressed the hardship caused by inflation and its commitment to returning it to 2 percent, likely requiring slower growth and softer labor-market conditions.

nodes.title: Monetary Policy
nodes.summary: Financial vulnerabilities remained moderate for households and businesses but elevated in real estate and parts of the nonbank financial sector. Three banks failed amid uninsured-deposit dependence, interest-rate-related asset losses, and weak risk management, although the broader banking system remained liquid and well-capitalized. Global activity rebounded early in 2023, inflation eased mainly through lower energy prices, and major foreign central banks generally continued tightening cautiously. The FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 5–5¼ percent while slowing the pace of increases and continued reducing its securities holdings by about $420 billion, partially offset by emergency bank liquidity support. Strong labor demand narrowed demographic employment and wage gaps, though disparities persisted. Bank credit conditions tightened and were expected to tighten further, potentially weighing unevenly on economic activity, especially in commercial real estate and small businesses. In response to March banking stress, discount-window borrowing rose, the BTFP was introduced, and Federal Reserve lending increased total assets despite continued portfolio reduction.

nodes.title: Special Topics
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve balance-sheet reduction, banking-sector liquidity support, labor-market disparities, tightening bank credit and its potentially uneven economic effects, developments in the SOMA portfolio and money-market facilities, and monetary policy rules. The Fed reduced securities holdings by about $420 billion while offsetting part of the decline with emergency-related lending, including the BTFP and discount window. Labor-market gains narrowed demographic disparities but did not eliminate them; bank lending tightened amid monetary policy and March 2023 stresses; and elevated inflation and tight employment conditions supported recommendations for high policy rates.

The June 2023 summary reviews easing but still-high inflation, modest and slowing economic growth, a very tight but cooling labor market, and tighter financial and credit conditions. It covers the FOMC’s rate increase to 5–5¼ percent, continued balance-sheet reduction, emergency lending through the discount window and BTFP, and the implications of monetary policy rules. The report assesses the failures of three banks and the resilience of the broader banking system, elevated real-estate and nonbank-finance vulnerabilities, tightening credit and its uneven effects, and developments in the SOMA portfolio and money-market facilities. It also discusses persistent labor-market disparities, rebounding global activity, continued foreign monetary tightening, and the Federal Reserve’s commitment to returning inflation to 2 percent even at the cost of slower growth and softer employment conditions.

structure.summary: The section reviews Federal Reserve assessments from June 2023 and March 2024, covering easing but above-target inflation, slowing or resilient economic activity, tight but cooling labor markets, and tightening financial and credit conditions. It explains the FOMC’s policy-rate decisions, balance-sheet runoff, emergency lending, ample-reserves operations, and the role of monetary policy rules in returning inflation to 2 percent. The section also examines banking failures and resilience, financial-stability risks in real estate and nonbank finance, money and housing markets, the SOMA portfolio, global developments, business and manufacturing activity, and persistent employment and earnings disparities.

structure.title: 3 Financial Stability

nodes.title: Monitoring Financial Vulnerabilities
Asset Valuation Pressures
nodes.summary: The text explains the Federal Reserve’s financial-stability framework, distinguishing unpredictable shocks from gradually accumulating vulnerabilities. It describes quarterly monitoring of asset valuations, borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and funding risk, and explains how the results inform regulatory, supervisory, monetary-policy, and interagency efforts. It also discusses the Federal Reserve’s Financial Stability Report and its transparency purpose. The main substantive focus is asset valuation pressure: high or overvalued assets can destabilize the system, especially when supported by leverage or other risks, so the Fed monitors multiple indicators. In 2023, valuations remained notable despite a strong economy, with elevated equity, residential real estate, commercial real estate, and farmland prices, while corporate credit spreads were relatively subdued. The text includes figures on S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratios and corporate bond spreads, and introduces excessive household and business borrowing as another vulnerability that can amplify shocks through reduced spending.

nodes.title: Borrowing by Households and Businesses
nodes.summary: The text assesses 2023 financial stability, finding elevated equity, residential real estate, commercial real estate, and farmland valuations, while corporate credit spreads were relatively subdued. Household and business debt burdens declined relative to GDP, though large firms remained leveraged and private credit expanded amid limited transparency. Businesses generally retained strong debt-servicing capacity, with only modest deterioration in credit quality. Household finances remained resilient, despite slight increases in consumer delinquencies and evolving student-loan repayment policies. Banks were broadly well capitalized and resilient after the March 2023 bank runs, supported by emergency interventions, but unrealized bond losses and commercial real estate exposure remained risks, particularly for smaller banks. The accompanying figures document equity valuation ratios, corporate bond spreads, private-sector credit relative to GDP, and bank common equity tier 1 ratios, with relevant historical definitions and sources.

nodes.title: Leverage in the Financial System
nodes.summary: The text assesses financial stability in 2023 across private credit, households, banks, insurers, hedge funds, and cash-management funds. Household debt and bank leverage risks were generally contained, and banks remained well capitalized and liquid, but opaque private-credit exposures, bank fair-value losses, commercial real estate risks, insurer investment exposures, elevated hedge-fund leverage, interest-rate mismatches, and growing money-market-sector assets remain vulnerabilities. It also presents and explains figures on bank capital ratios and liquid assets, including their categories, definitions, historical coverage, recession markers, and Federal Reserve data sources, and notes the March 2023 banking intervention and the expiration of the BTFP.

nodes.title: Funding Risk
nodes.summary: The text reviews financial-stability vulnerabilities outside and within banking, describing elevated hedge-fund leverage, rising risk-taking by life insurers, and banks’ still-ample but somewhat reduced liquidity, alongside persistent interest-rate risk and the expiration of the BTFP. It presents data on bank liquid assets and explains the measures and institutions covered. It then discusses growth in money market and other cash-management funds, SEC reforms, orderly bond-fund redemptions, and the systemic risks posed by large stablecoin holdings and weak oversight. Finally, it describes Federal Reserve cooperation and the FSOC’s mandate, structure, 2023 priorities, and monitoring initiatives for hedge funds and nonbank mortgage servicers.

The section explains the Federal Reserve's quarterly framework for monitoring four financial-stability vulnerabilities—asset valuations, household and business borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and funding risk—and how the analysis supports policy, supervision, research, transparency, and interagency action. It relates financial-sector resilience to the condition of households and businesses and explains the consequences of shocks in stable versus unstable systems. For 2023, it finds elevated equity, residential and commercial real estate, and farmland valuations; generally reduced household and business debt burdens but risks from large-firm leverage and opaque private credit; resilient households, businesses, and well-capitalized banks despite delinquencies, bond losses, commercial real estate exposure, and the March banking turmoil; and contained overall bank and household leverage alongside vulnerabilities involving insurers, hedge funds, private credit, interest-rate mismatches, and money-market assets. It also reviews bank liquidity, funding pressures, the expiration of emergency support, cash-management funds, SEC reforms, stablecoins, and nonbank risks, while presenting supporting valuation, credit-spread, leverage, capital, and liquidity figures with their definitions, coverage, historical context, and sources, and describing the Federal Reserve's and FSOC's monitoring and coordination efforts.

nodes.title: Domestic and International Cooperation and Coordination
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2023 financial-stability developments, noting declining corporate bond mutual-fund holdings and orderly redemptions, as well as persistent stablecoin-related vulnerabilities and potential spillovers. It describes Federal Reserve cooperation through the FSOC and FSB, including FSOC's mandate, structure, systemic-risk monitoring, four priorities, work on nonbanks, Treasury markets, climate risks, digital assets, new designation and analytical guidance, and its 2023 annual report. It also explains the FSB's role in global coordination and its 2023 work on open-end fund liquidity mismatches, crypto-asset intermediaries, and nonbank financial resilience.

structure.summary: This section explains how the Federal Reserve promotes financial stability through monitoring vulnerabilities, informing policy and supervision, addressing systemic spillovers from large institutions, and coordinating with domestic and international partners. It describes the 2023 assessment of valuations, borrowing, leverage, funding, bank and nonbank resilience, liquidity and funding pressures, commercial real estate, private credit, stablecoins, money-market assets, and other risks, supported by detailed figures and monitoring methods. It also reviews cooperation through the FSOC and FSB on systemic-risk oversight, nonbanks, Treasury markets, climate risks, digital assets, fund liquidity, crypto intermediaries, and broader financial resilience, while directing related monetary-policy and supervision material to other sections.

structure.title: 4 Supervision and Regulation

nodes.title: Box 4.1. Banking Sector Conditions
nodes.summary: This section describes the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation mission, including overseeing financial institutions, developing regulatory policy and acting on banking applications, and analyzing banking-sector data. It references the semiannual Supervision and Regulation Report on banking conditions and identifies the broad range and number of entities supervised, including an explanation of Edge Act and agreement corporations.

nodes.title: Supervised and Regulated Institutions
State Member Banks
nodes.summary: The text presents the Federal Reserve's 2023 framework for categorizing supervised banking organizations by size and type. It reports the number, branch presence, and U.S. market and asset shares of Federal Reserve and state member banks, then summarizes Table 4.1's portfolios—LISCC, LFBO, RBO, CBO, and SLHC—including their definitions, institution counts, total assets, state member bank subsets, and footnotes on holding-company composition.

nodes.title: Bank Holding Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics on U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, and Federal Reserve-supervised insurance-focused SLHCs. It describes their numbers, asset levels, subsidiaries, activities, regulatory oversight, and the distribution of domestic FHCs by asset size. It also outlines the Federal Reserve’s risk-based insurance supervision framework and its 2023 implementation, and introduces financial market utilities as operators of multilateral systems for transferring, clearing, and settling financial transactions.

nodes.title: Savings and Loan Holding Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics on U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, and savings and loan holding companies, including their numbers, ownership, asset levels, activities, and regulatory oversight. It also describes Federal Reserve supervision of insurance-focused SLHCs and the implementation of a new risk-based insurance supervisory framework, then begins defining financial market utilities as operators of multilateral financial transfer, clearing, and settlement systems.

nodes.title: Financial Market Utilities
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 statistics and regulatory arrangements for U.S. bank holding companies, financial holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, insurance-focused SLHCs, financial market utilities, and international banking operations. It details their numbers, asset holdings, organizational structures, regulators, and supervisory developments, including the Federal Reserve's insurance framework, oversight of systemically important FMUs under Dodd-Frank and Regulation HH, U.S. banks' foreign branches, Edge Act corporations, and foreign banks' U.S. operations.

nodes.title: International Activities
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s oversight of designated and other financial market utilities, including its expanded Dodd-Frank responsibilities and Regulation HH requirements. It reports 2023 international banking activities involving U.S. banks abroad, Edge Act corporations, and foreign banks operating in the United States, along with related examination totals. It explains the Federal Reserve’s risk-based supervisory framework, priorities, and examination practices, and discusses its response to the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures, including the SVB review, identified vulnerabilities, and efforts to make supervision faster, more risk-sensitive, and forward-looking. It concludes with 2023 examination and inspection figures for state member banks and holding companies.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s supervised and regulated institutions in 2023, covering the classification, scale, assets, activities, organizational structures, and oversight of state member banks, bank and financial holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, and insurance-focused SLHCs. It explains the Federal Reserve’s risk-based insurance supervision framework, introduces financial market utilities and their Dodd-Frank and Regulation HH oversight, and describes international banking operations involving U.S. and foreign banks. The section also outlines supervisory priorities and examination practices, discusses lessons and reforms following the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures, and reports examination and inspection activity for banks and holding companies.

nodes.title: Supervisory Developments
Supervisory and Regulatory Initiatives
Specialized Examinations
key_items: Government and Municipal Securities Dealers and Brokers
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve's specialized supervisory examinations and related activities in 2023, including stress testing and capital planning, fiduciary and transfer-agent oversight, government and municipal securities regulation, securities-credit lender examinations, and operational resilience, information technology, and cybersecurity support. It reports examination counts, applicable laws and rules, the 2023 stress-test results and capital-buffer framework, the exploratory market shock for global systemically important banks, and the categories of stress-testing publications issued.

nodes.title: Operational Resilience, Information Technology, and Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 supervision of fiduciary activities, transfer agents, government and municipal securities dealers, and securities-credit lenders, including examination totals and Regulation U responsibilities. It describes efforts to strengthen operational resilience through third-party risk guidance, educational sessions, IT and cybersecurity examinations, technology-provider oversight, and extensive domestic and international coordination on cyber, cloud, and incident-reporting issues. It also introduces the Novel Activities Supervision Program for crypto-assets, distributed ledger technology, and technology-based nonbank partnerships, and summarizes the agencies’ warning about key risks associated with crypto-sector activities.

nodes.title: Crypto-Asset Supervision
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervision initiatives and guidance on emerging operational, crypto-asset, and climate-related risks. It covers the launch and scope of the Novel Activities Supervision Program; interagency warnings about crypto risks, liquidity, and dollar-token activities; the process and risk areas for state member banks seeking supervisory nonobjection; the Federal Reserve’s exploratory climate scenario analysis exercise; final climate-risk management principles for large institutions; and the Federal Reserve’s enforcement authority over unsafe practices and violations. It also references Financial Stability Board publications on third-party risk management and cyber incident reporting.

nodes.title: Climate-Related Financial Risks
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervisory developments concerning crypto-asset activities, including a liquidity-risk statement and the 2023 supervisory nonobjection process for state member banks engaging in certain dollar-token activities, with attention to operational, cybersecurity, liquidity, illicit-finance, and consumer-compliance risks. It then discusses the Board’s exploratory 2023 climate scenario analysis exercise and finalized climate-related financial-risk management principles for institutions with at least $100 billion in assets, covering governance, planning, risk management, reporting, scenario analysis, and traditional risk categories. Finally, it introduces the Federal Reserve’s enforcement authority over supervised institutions and affiliated parties for unsafe or unsound practices and legal or regulatory violations, including cease-and-desist orders.

nodes.title: Enforcement Actions
key_items: Financial Disclosures by State Member Banks
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervision of crypto-asset activities, including liquidity-risk concerns and the supervisory nonobjection process for state member banks engaging in dollar-token activities. It covers the Board’s exploratory 2023 climate scenario analysis and finalized climate-risk management principles for large institutions. It then explains Federal Reserve enforcement authority, the formal and informal actions completed in 2023, civil penalties and their disposition, public availability of enforcement actions, and related responsibilities for securities-use disclosures and credit. Finally, it outlines state member bank financial-disclosure requirements and the independent two-level internal appeals process for material supervisory determinations, including the first-level review criteria and panel structure.

nodes.title: Internal Appeals of Material Super visory Determinations
nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve’s 2023 enforcement activity, including formal and informal actions, civil money penalties, public disclosure of enforcement orders, and related responsibilities involving bank financial disclosures and securities credit. It explains reporting requirements for certain state member banks and details the two-level internal appeals process for material supervisory determinations, including 2023 appeal activity. It also describes supervision and regulation assessments imposed on large banking organizations and FSOC-designated nonbank firms, noting the $771.1 million transferred to the Treasury. Finally, it covers the Federal Reserve’s training, technical assistance, and outreach for foreign supervisors and minority-owned institutions, including 20 seminars attended by about 900 officials and two events organized with the IMF and World Bank.

nodes.title: Assessments for Supervision and Regulation
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s MSD appeals process and reports one appeal and one filing extension in 2023. It explains supervision and regulation assessments for large bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, and certain FSOC-designated nonbank financial companies, noting that $771.1 million collected from 53 institutions was transferred to the Treasury rather than treated as Board revenue or used for expenses. It also covers the Federal Reserve’s training, technical assistance, and outreach activities, including 20 international and domestic seminars attended by about 900 foreign supervisors and two events organized with the IMF and World Bank.

nodes.title: Training and Technical Assistance
key_items: Efforts to Support Minority-Owned Depository Institutions
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervisory appeals and 2023 appeal activity; supervision and regulation assessments collected for the Treasury; international supervisory training and technical assistance; the Partnership for Progress program and 2023 initiatives supporting minority depository institutions; and the Federal Reserve’s international engagement through the Financial Stability Board, including its 2023 priorities and publications on financial stability, decentralized finance, commodities markets, and crypto-assets.

nodes.title: International Engagement
Financial Stability Board
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve supervisory outreach to MDIs and CDFIs through banking conferences and webinars on funding programs and ECIP requirements, including ECIP's purpose and nearly $9 billion in Treasury support. It then reviews the Federal Reserve's international engagement through the FSB and BCBS, outlining 2023 priorities and publications on financial stability, cross-border payments, crypto-assets, open-ended funds, third-party risk, non-bank leverage, Basel III implementation, climate risks, digitalization, banking turmoil, and emerging risks. It also explains the roles and membership of the FSB and BCBS and directs readers to their publication resources.

nodes.title: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 involvement in international financial-stability, banking-supervision, and payment-infrastructure work. It lists key FSB publications on non-bank leverage, cross-border payments, third-party risk, and open-ended-fund liquidity mismatch; describes BCBS priorities and final and consultative publications concerning Basel III, banking turmoil, climate and cryptoasset risks, data, disclosures, and supervisory principles; and outlines CPMI collaboration with the FSB and IOSCO on cross-border payments, financial-market infrastructures, central-counterparty losses, margining, and implementation of market-infrastructure principles. It also provides publication-list links and notes the BCBS membership structure.

nodes.title: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 international supervisory and regulatory engagement through the BCBS, CPMI, and IAIS. It lists representative BCBS publications and consultations, describes CPMI’s cross-border payments, financial-market-infrastructure, and IOSCO-coordinated work along with its 2023 publications and consultation, and outlines the Federal Reserve’s IAIS participation, 2023 insurance-supervision initiatives, and a related IAIS issues paper. Links to the cited documents and complete publication catalogs are provided.

nodes.title: International Association of Insurance Supervisors
nodes.summary: The text catalogs 2023 CPMI publications and one consultative document on payment systems and related financial-market topics, then describes the Federal Reserve’s participation in IAIS insurance-standard setting, IAIS initiatives and selected publications, and the advisory work of the IPAC, including life-insurer liquidity and climate issues. It concludes by explaining the interagency Shared National Credit program, its review schedule and participating agencies, and provides links to relevant publication, program, and committee information.

The section surveys the Federal Reserve’s domestic outreach and broad international financial-stability, banking-supervision, payments, market-infrastructure, and insurance-regulatory engagement. It covers MDI and CDFI outreach and ECIP, then details work through the FSB, BCBS, CPMI, IOSCO, and IAIS on topics including Basel III, cross-border payments, nonbank leverage, cryptoassets, climate and digital risks, banking turmoil, fund liquidity, third-party risk, financial-market infrastructures, and insurance supervision. It also discusses the relevant organizations’ roles and memberships, advisory work on life-insurer liquidity and climate issues, the Shared National Credit program, and links to cited publications and information resources.

nodes.title: Shared National Credit Program
nodes.summary: The text lists key 2023 IAIS consultations and guidance on insurance capital standards, aggregation-method comparability, valuation, capital adequacy, and climate risk, with links to these documents and the full IAIS publications archive. It describes the Federal Reserve’s IPAC role and 2023 activities, including comments on the ICS consultation, assessment of life-insurer liquidity amid rising rates, and creation of a climate insurance working group. It then explains the interagency Shared National Credit program, its participating agencies, scope, review schedule, and differing annual review frequencies for large and other agent banks.

nodes.title: Bank Secrecy Act and Anti-Money-Laundering Compliance
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Federal Reserve supervised BSA/AML compliance, helped update the FFIEC examination manual, supported implementation of the 2020 AML Act, and participated in the Treasury-led BSA Advisory Group. It also coordinated internationally on sanctions, AML, and counter-terrorist financing, including sanctions related to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, contributed to Financial Action Task Force standards, and supported Financial Stability Board work on the G20 cross-border payments roadmap progress report.

nodes.title: International Coordination on Sanctions, Anti-Money-Laundering, and Counter-Terrorism Financing
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 BSA/AML supervisory responsibilities, participation in updates to the FFIEC examination manual and implementation of the AML Act, and involvement in the Treasury-led BSA Advisory Group. It covers extensive international coordination on sanctions, AML/CFT, and cross-border payments through the FATF, FSB, BIS, and bilateral and regional engagements, including information sharing and technical training. It also explains Federal Reserve regulatory reporting requirements for holding companies and other banking organizations, the purposes of those reports, the entities covered, and 2023 revisions to the FR Y-7Q report concerning U.S. asset calculations, filing requirements, deadlines, and related clarifications.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s supervisory and regulatory work in 2023, including risk-based examinations and inspections of domestic and foreign banks, holding companies, and specialized financial activities; supervisory responses to the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank; stress testing, capital planning, operational resilience, technology, cybersecurity, and third-party risk oversight; and initiatives addressing crypto-assets, dollar-token activities, and climate-related financial risks. It explains enforcement actions, penalties, disclosures, regulatory reporting, internal appeals, and assessments transferred to the Treasury. The section also covers training and outreach for foreign and minority institutions, domestic programs such as the Shared National Credit program, and extensive international engagement on banking, insurance, financial stability, payments, market infrastructures, Basel standards, nonbank finance, crypto-assets, climate and digital risks, sanctions, AML/CFT, and cross-border payments.

nodes.title: Regulatory Reports
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s international AML/CFT cooperation and training, its regulatory-reporting requirements and the 2023 revisions to Federal Reserve reporting forms, and corresponding FFIEC reporting changes following the mandated Call Report review. It explains the purposes and affected filers of these reports, provides effective dates and key changes for each form, and concludes with the Federal Reserve’s staff-development program for nearly 4,200 supervisory professionals and state-agency staff.

nodes.title: Staff Development Programs
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 changes to Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory reporting, including revisions to the FR 2590, Call Reports, and FFIEC 002, with their effective dates and statutory and approval processes. It explains the purpose of uniform FFIEC reports and summarizes Federal Reserve staff development, 2023 training activities and delivery methods, examiner commissioning tracks and results, and continuing professional development resources for Federal Reserve and state supervisory personnel.

The section surveys the Federal Reserve’s 2023 supervisory and regulatory activities, including risk-based examinations, responses to major bank failures, stress testing, capital and operational resilience, technology and cybersecurity oversight, third-party risk, crypto-assets, dollar-token activities, climate risks, enforcement, reporting, appeals, and Treasury assessments. It also covers domestic and international outreach and cooperation on banking, insurance, financial stability, payments, market infrastructures, Basel standards, nonbank finance, sanctions, AML/CFT, and cross-border payments. In addition, it details AML/CFT training, revisions to Federal Reserve and FFIEC regulatory reports and Call Reports, their purposes, filers, approval processes, effective dates and key changes, and staff-development, examiner commissioning, training, and continuing-education programs for Federal Reserve and state supervisory personnel.

nodes.title: Regulatory Developments
key_items: Public Notice of Federal Reserve Decisions and Filings Received
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s regulatory functions and summarizes its 2023 rulemakings, statements, supervisory letters, guidance, proposals, and final actions. These covered crypto-asset and liquidity risks, bank stress tests and the Silicon Valley Bank review, LIBOR transition, supervisory technology, valuation standards, third-party risk, commercial real estate, capital and resolution requirements, liquidity planning, anti-money-laundering examinations, novel activities and dollar tokens, Community Reinvestment Act rules, climate-related financial risks, debit-card interchange fees, consumer-credit and appraisal thresholds, payment-service pricing, reserve requirements, investment-fund reporting, and beneficial-ownership information. The text also explains that the Federal Reserve acted on 752 banking applications in 2023, publishes semiannual application-activity reports, and provides online notices of decisions and application-submission guidance.

structure.summary: This section reviews the Federal Reserve’s supervision and regulation responsibilities, banking-sector conditions, and the institutions and financial market utilities it oversees, including domestic and international banking organizations and insurance-related entities. It covers supervisory priorities and examinations, responses to major bank failures, risk-based insurance supervision, stress testing, resilience, technology and cybersecurity, third-party and climate risks, crypto and dollar-token activities, enforcement, reporting, AML/CFT, examiner training, and domestic and international cooperation. It also summarizes 2023 regulatory actions and guidance across capital, liquidity, resolution, market, consumer, climate, payments, AML, reporting, and novel-activity issues, and describes banking-application decisions, reporting, and public application resources.

structure.title: 5 Payment System and Reserve Bank Oversight

nodes.title: Payment Services to Depository and Other Institutions
Commercial Check-Collection Service
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank priced payment services, including check collection, ACH, funds and securities transfers, multilateral settlement, and 24/7 instant-payment support. It explains the creation of Federal Reserve Financial Services to integrate and strengthen these offerings following financial-sector changes and the 2023 FedNow® launch. It details the commercial check-collection service and its 2023 financial and processing results, including cost recovery, revenue, expenses, income, check volumes, values, and expected continued decline. It also describes the commercial ACH service's domestic, cross-border, same-day, and next-day electronic batch-payment capabilities, and defines depository institutions and their role in the economy and Federal Reserve payment system.

nodes.title: Commercial Automated Clearinghouse Service
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank priced payment services and their consolidation under Federal Reserve Financial Services following financial-sector changes and the 2023 FedNow® launch. It details the commercial check-collection service, including its offerings, 2023 costs, revenue, recovery rate, income, processing volumes, declining trends, and outlook, and introduces the commercial ACH service for domestic and cross-border batch payments. It also defines depository institutions and notes their broader economic and payment-system roles.

nodes.title: Box 5.1. Priced Services and Cost Recovery
FedNow Service
nodes.summary: The text presents 2021–23 activity and cost-recovery results for Federal Reserve priced payment and securities services, including declining commercial-check and Fedwire-funds volumes, growing commercial ACH activity, stable National Settlement entries, and a major 2023 increase in Fedwire securities activity following the inclusion of Treasury securities. It details 2023 ACH and Fedwire financial results and volumes, describes the July 2023 launch, adoption, purpose, implementation cost, and expected growth of the FedNow instant-payments service, and explains the functions, activity, values, and financial performance of Fedwire Funds and the National Settlement Service. It also defines the measurement categories and notes the 2023 change in the priced Fedwire Securities scope.

nodes.title: Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services
nodes.summary: The text reports the Federal Reserve's $545 million investment in FedNow and its planned future publication of transaction volumes; summarizes the 2023 cost recovery and financial results for Fedwire Funds and National Settlement Services; describes the purpose and 2023 activity of the Fedwire Funds Service, including transfer volumes and values; explains the National Settlement Service and its files, entries, arrangements, and settlement value; and introduces the Fedwire Securities Service as a central securities depository and real-time settlement system for certain government-related and international securities, with its description incomplete in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Fedwire Securities Service
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve payment-system services and oversight, including the $545 million implementation of FedNow and its planned future transaction reporting. It reports 2023 cost recovery, expenses, revenues, and performance for Fedwire Funds and the National Settlement Service, explains their functions, and provides their transaction volumes and values. It also explains the Fedwire Securities Service, its expanded 2023 priced component that included Treasury securities, its financial and activity results, securities transfers, principal and interest payments, and securities held and outstanding. Finally, it describes the six fee-based FedLine Solutions used to access Reserve Bank services and their connectivity, security, contingency, and modernization purposes.

nodes.title: FedLine Solutions: Access to Reserve Bank Services
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 activity and financial results for the Fedwire Securities Service, including its expanded Treasury-security coverage, cost recovery, revenues, expenses, transfers, payment values, and securities held. It describes FedLine Solutions and the migration from legacy access products, then explains Federal Reserve intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, their role in payment efficiency and risk reduction, and why their use and fees remain low under the ample-reserves framework and related policy changes.

nodes.title: Federal Reserve Intraday Credit
nodes.summary: The text discusses Federal Reserve oversight of intraday credit, defining daylight overdrafts and explaining their benefits for payment efficiency and risk reduction. It reports that peak and average overdrafts, as well as related fees, remained low from 2007 to 2023 and are expected to stay low because of high overnight reserve balances, the ample-reserves regime, and the 2011 elimination of fees for collateralized overdrafts. It also notes the Payment System Risk policy's provision of no-cost, collateralized intraday credit to healthy institutions and mentions legacy payment-product price increases and discontinuations such as FedMail Fax.

The section explains how the Federal Reserve prices payment and settlement services to recover direct, indirect, imputed, and private-sector-equivalent costs, and reports decade-long and 2023 cost-recovery results, accounting adjustments, and the special treatment of FedNow. It reviews the launch, investment, adoption, and expected development of FedNow; the purposes, activity, financial performance, and settlement functions of ACH, checks, Fedwire Funds, National Settlement, and Fedwire Securities services; and the 2023 expansion of priced Fedwire Securities activity to Treasury securities. It also describes FedLine access products and their modernization, and discusses intraday credit and daylight overdrafts, including their payment-system benefits, low recent usage and fees under the ample-reserves regime, collateralized-credit policy, and changes to legacy payment products.

The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s priced payment and settlement services and their consolidation under Federal Reserve Financial Services, covering commercial check collection and ACH capabilities, 2023 financial and processing results, and the role of depository institutions. It explains pricing and cost-recovery principles and results, including FedNow’s launch and treatment, and surveys the activities and performance of ACH, check, Fedwire Funds, National Settlement, and Fedwire Securities services, including expanded Treasury securities processing. It also covers FedLine access modernization and the policies, usage, fees, benefits, and recent changes associated with intraday credit and daylight overdrafts.

nodes.title: Currency and Coin
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 currency and coin operations, noting the distribution, return, net payment, and outstanding-value trends for Federal Reserve notes, as well as coin distribution and returns. It describes modernization of the U.S. Currency Program through NextGen processing equipment, regional cash-processing studies, facility replacements and upgrades, a new BEP production plant, and development of a secure next banknote family beginning with the $10 note targeted for 2026. It also covers counterfeit-deterrence research, the CEP’s global education and outreach results, and the Board’s collaboration with domestic and international central-bank and cash-machine organizations to protect currency security, usability, availability, and public confidence.

nodes.title: Fiscal Agency and Government Depository Services
Payment Services
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve Banks’ role as fiscal agents and depositories for the Treasury and other entities, including payment, financing and securities, accounting and reporting, technology, and operating-cash services. It reports 2021–23 reimbursable expenses and explains that 2023 expenses fell mainly because of lower pension costs and the discontinuation of electronic tax collection. It details Treasury payment systems such as Stored Value Card services and Pay.gov, including their functions, users, transaction volumes, and dollar values, and outlines financing and securities support, including Treasury auctions, marketable securities, and savings bonds. The excerpt ends while continuing the discussion of 2023 Treasury securities auctions.

nodes.title: Financing and Securities Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank services provided for the Treasury, covering payment processing, military stored-value cards, Pay.gov, Treasury financing and securities operations, government accounting and reporting, and supporting technology infrastructure. It reports 2023 transaction volumes, service expenses and year-over-year changes, explains the main causes of those changes, identifies key systems and programs, and provides footnotes on Treasury product demand, Fedwire accounting, and official government financial reports.

nodes.title: Accounting and Reporting Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank support for Treasury securities, accounting, reporting, and technology infrastructure. It reports 2023 expenses of $194.4 million for financing and securities services, a 6.4 percent decrease related to changes in Fedwire Securities Service accounting, and $81.1 million for financial accounting and reporting, a 10.3 percent increase driven by technical-debt remediation, cybersecurity, and cloud migration. It explains the roles of the Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing, outlines Treasury financial publications supported by the Reserve Banks, notes a 164 percent increase in demand for Treasury products, and provides related footnotes and publication links.

nodes.title: Infrastructure and Technology Services
nodes.summary: The text describes Reserve Bank support for Treasury securities issuance and servicing, accounting and reporting, infrastructure and technology, and banking services for other entities, including 2023 expenses and the reasons for their changes. It explains key systems such as the Cash Accounting Reporting System and G-Invoicing, cloud migration and cybersecurity efforts, services for Ginnie Mae and other organizations, and the Federal Reserve’s broader roles as payment-system supervisor, regulator, researcher, and improvement catalyst. It also summarizes the Federal Reserve’s payment-system research activities and provides explanatory footnotes and links to major Treasury reports and the Cloud Smart strategy.

nodes.title: Services Provided to Other Entities
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Reserve Banks advanced cloud migration, infrastructure automation, lifecycle planning, and cybersecurity, reducing infrastructure and technology expenses to $143.6 million. They also provided U.S.-dollar banking and electronic securities services to other entities, with expenses declining to $14.9 million. The Federal Reserve additionally acts as a payment-system supervisor, regulator, researcher, and catalyst for improvements, researching payment, clearing, settlement, and financial market infrastructures and their role in the broader economy.

This section describes the Federal Reserve Banks’ fiscal-agent and depository services for the Treasury and other entities, covering payment processing, stored-value cards, Pay.gov, Treasury financing and securities operations, accounting and reporting, technology infrastructure, and banking services. It presents 2021–23 and 2023 expenses, transaction activity, and the reasons for major year-over-year changes, including pension costs, discontinued electronic tax collection, accounting changes, technical-debt remediation, cybersecurity, and cloud migration. It explains key systems and Treasury reports, services for Ginnie Mae and other organizations, increased demand for Treasury products, and the Federal Reserve’s supervisory, regulatory, research, and improvement roles in payment and financial market infrastructures, with related explanatory footnotes and links.

nodes.title: Evolutions and Improvements to the System
Payment System Research and Analysis
nodes.summary: The text reports the Reserve Banks' 2023 cloud migration, infrastructure and cybersecurity efforts, related expenses, and banking and securities services provided to other entities and their costs. It then describes the Federal Reserve's broader payment-system roles in operations, supervision, regulation, research, and improvement. Research covered payment trends, innovation, financial market infrastructures, and fraud, while digital-innovation work examined digital assets, CBDCs, cross-border and wholesale payments, associated policy and technology implications, and collaboration with international and domestic stakeholders. Finally, it explains the Board's statutory payment-system regulatory responsibilities and cites relevant online resources.

nodes.title: Digital Innovations Research
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve oversight and research on payment systems. Its 2023 research covered payment-method trends, payment innovations such as instant payments and digital assets, financial market infrastructure, and payments fraud. It explains broader staff research into digital assets, CBDCs, cross-border and wholesale settlement technologies, and the policy, technological, and infrastructure implications of innovation. The Federal Reserve works with international institutions, central banks, and domestic stakeholders on topics including tokenization, distributed ledgers, APIs, and digital payments. Finally, it notes the Board’s congressional responsibility to implement laws governing banking and payment systems through regulations and provides links to relevant research and regulatory resources.

nodes.title: Payment System Regulation
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve oversight, research, regulation, and modernization of the payment system. It covers 2023 research on payment-method trends, innovations, infrastructure, and fraud; digital-asset and payment-technology research and related domestic and international collaboration; the Board's statutory regulatory role; a proposed reduction and biennial adjustment process for debit-card interchange fees under Regulation II; the public Master Account and Services Database; implementation of FedNow; technology, cybersecurity, FedLine, currency-processing, and IT modernization initiatives; and the refreshed 2024–26 System IT Strategic Plan. It also provides references to relevant Federal Reserve websites and studies.

nodes.title: Other Improvements and Efforts
nodes.summary: The text describes 2023 regulatory and transparency initiatives, including proposed debit-card interchange-fee changes under Regulation II and the public database for Reserve Bank master-account and service access. It reviews Reserve Bank modernization efforts involving FedNow, payment-processing platforms, currency equipment, IT strategy, datacenters, cybersecurity, and facility infrastructure, and directs readers to financial information in table G.13. It also explains Board oversight, independent audits of the combined and individual Reserve Bank financial statements, and use of the COSO framework for evaluating financial-reporting controls.

The section reviews Federal Reserve improvements to the payment system, covering Reserve Bank cloud, infrastructure, cybersecurity, banking, and securities-service activities and costs; the System’s operational, supervisory, regulatory, and research roles; research and collaboration on payment trends, fraud, digital assets, CBDCs, instant, cross-border, and wholesale payments, and emerging technologies; and the Board’s statutory regulatory responsibilities. It also discusses Regulation II debit-card interchange-fee proposals, transparency through the Master Account and Services Database, FedNow implementation, payment, currency, IT, cybersecurity, datacenter, and facility modernization, the 2024–26 System IT Strategic Plan, and financial oversight through disclosures, independent audits, and COSO-based control assessments, with references to relevant resources.

nodes.title: Oversight of Federal Reserve Banks
Income and Expenses
nodes.summary: The text describes the Board's annual oversight and auditing of SOMA and foreign-currency activities, including compliance, technology, controls, and reporting to the FOMC. It presents the Reserve Banks' combined 2023 financial results, showing sharply higher expenses and a large net loss compared with 2022, explains the statutory process for Treasury remittances and deferred assets when earnings are inadequate, notes that $670 million was transferred to the Treasury in 2023, and outlines the detailed income, expense, adjustment, distribution, and comprehensive-income categories in Table 5.3. It also identifies the detailed financial, budgetary, employment, and historical data provided in Appendix G and explains the purposes of the relevant assessments and income categories.

nodes.title: SOMA Holdings
nodes.summary: The text describes SOMA’s role in holding securities acquired through New York Fed open market operations, identifies the types of holdings, references a table comparing SOMA financial measures for 2023 and 2022, reports 2023 balances and interest rates for major Reserve Bank lending programs, and explains additional pandemic-related lending through special purpose vehicles. It also refers readers to appendix G, table G.2, for detailed Treasury and federal agency securities holdings.

nodes.title: Lending
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s SOMA operations and lending programs, including the New York Fed’s role in executing FOMC-directed open market transactions, the securities and investments held, and pandemic-related lending through special purpose vehicles. It presents 2023 lending balances and rates and summarizes, through Table 5.4, SOMA assets, liabilities, net holdings, income or expenses, interest rates, and year-over-year changes for 2023 and 2022, with supporting definitions and accounting notes.

This section describes Reserve Bank technology, cybersecurity, and facility modernization efforts, then explains the independent audits, COSO-based internal-control assessments, KPMG engagements, auditor-independence safeguards, and the Board's ongoing and comprehensive oversight of Reserve Banks and related Federal Reserve operations. It also covers oversight and financial reporting for SOMA and foreign-currency activities; Reserve Bank income, expenses, losses, Treasury remittances, deferred assets, and supporting data; SOMA's securities holdings and open-market role; and Federal Reserve lending programs, including pandemic-related special purpose vehicles, 2023 balances and rates, and comparative SOMA financial information.

nodes.title: Pro Forma Financial Statements for Federal Reserve Priced Services
Notes to Pro Forma Financial Statements for Priced Services
(1) Short-Term Assets
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and financing of priced-service assets, including receivables, collection items, float costs, specialized and shared long-term assets, and related deferred taxes. They describe the matched-book funding structure and imputed equity levels used to meet FDIC capitalization requirements, including a revision to the 2022 figure, and introduce the Board's Payment System Risk policy and its basis in international financial-market-infrastructure standards applicable to Fedwire Services.

nodes.title: (2) Long-Term Assets
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and accounting treatment of short-term and long-term priced-service assets, including receivables, collection items, float, shared assets, deferred taxes, and Board-related assets. They describe the matched-book financing structure and imputed equity requirements for 2023 and 2022, note the revision to the 2022 figure, and introduce the Board's Payment System Risk policy and its basis in international financial market infrastructure standards.

nodes.title: (3) Liabilities and Equity
nodes.summary: The notes explain the composition and financing of priced-service assets, liabilities, and equity; the treatment of collection float, deferred taxes, pension obligations, and risk-management capital; the Payment System Risk policy and required liquid assets; and the recognition of revenue and operating expenses. They provide applicable 2023 and 2022 equity, tax, pension, Board-expense, and service-cost amounts, identify exclusions such as FedNow development, and note related prior-year revisions and ASC 715 requirements.

nodes.title: (4) Revenue
nodes.summary: The text explains Fedwire Funds risk-management and capital/liquidity provisions, including the six-month operating-expense requirement and the absence of required imputed balances in 2023 and 2022. It describes ASC 715 accounting for pension and other benefit plans, related pension assets, deferred taxes, and AOCI changes, including a restatement of the 2022 pension asset. It defines priced-services revenue and operating expenses, identifies the services and Board costs covered, excludes FedNow development costs, and reports qualified and nonqualified pension service costs for 2023 and 2022, along with the 2019 ASC 715 disaggregation update.

nodes.title: (5) Operating Expenses
nodes.summary: The text explains Fedwire Funds risk-management and capital requirements, pension accounting under ASC 715, and the revenue and operating-expense structure of Reserve Bank priced services. It reports pension assets, funded-status effects, Board and pension expenses, exclusions for FedNow development, and the presentation of service-level income statements. It then describes imputed costs under the PSAF model—including taxes, equity returns, debt interest, sales taxes, and float interest—along with their assumptions, allocation methods, daily average float-recovery data for 2023 and 2022, relevant footnotes, and the definition of credit float.

nodes.title: (6) Imputed Costs
nodes.summary: The passage explains Reserve Bank service-accounting treatment under ASC 715, the components and calculation methods for imputed costs under the PSAF model, allocation of debt interest, treatment and recovery of credit float, related 2023–2022 float figures and adjustments, the composition of other income from imputed investments, and the formula for annual cost recovery.

nodes.title: (7) Other Income and Expenses
nodes.summary:
Payment System and Reserve Bank Oversight 81
Float that is created by account adjustments due to transaction errors and the observance of non- standard holidays by some depository institutions was recovered from the depository institutions through charging institutions directly. Float subject to recovery is valued at the federal funds rate. Certain ACH funding requirements and check products generate credit float; this float has been subtracted from the cost base subject to recovery in 2023 and 2022.
(7) Other Income and Expenses
Other income consists of income on imputed investments. Excess financing resulting from addi- tional equity imputed to meet the FDIC well-capitalized requirements is assumed to be invested and earning interest at the 3-month Treasury bill rate.
(8) Cost Recovery
Annual cost recovery is the ratio of revenue, including other income, to the sum of operating expenses, imputed costs, imputed income taxes, and after-tax targeted return on equity.
