The section describes the assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses, and financing of Reserve Bank priced services, including matched-book funding, imputed equity, FDIC capitalization requirements, and related 2022 revisions. It covers the Payment System Risk policy and Fedwire liquidity requirements; ASC 715 treatment of pensions, deferred taxes, funded status, AOCI, and service costs; recognition and presentation of service revenue and expenses, including Board costs and the exclusion of FedNow development. It explains PSAF imputed taxes, debt and equity costs, sales taxes, investment income, and float recovery, including credit float from ACH, checks, transaction errors, and holidays, with 2023–2022 calculations and allocation assumptions. Finally, it defines other income from imputed investments and the annual cost-recovery ratio.

This section presents 2023 and 2022 pro forma financial statements for Federal Reserve priced services, including consolidated and service-level balance sheets and income statements covering assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, operating and imputed costs, taxes, other income, net income, targeted returns, and cost recovery. The accompanying notes explain funding and capitalization, Payment System Risk and Fedwire liquidity requirements, pension and deferred-tax accounting, revenue and expense recognition, Board and nonpriced-service costs, FedNow exclusions, and the calculation and allocation of imputed taxes, debt and equity costs, sales taxes, investment income, and float recovery, including credit-float sources and annual cost-recovery measures.

structure.summary: The section explains how the Federal Reserve supports and oversees the U.S. payment and settlement system through priced payment services, currency and coin distribution, fiscal-agent and government-depository operations, payment-system research and modernization, and comprehensive Reserve Bank oversight. It covers the 2023 launch and performance of FedNow and other payment services; currency production, processing, security, and distribution; Treasury and other agency services and their financial and operational developments; research and regulatory initiatives involving payments, technology, cybersecurity, digital assets, and emerging payment methods; audits, internal controls, SOMA, lending, income, expenses, and remittances; and detailed 2022–23 pro forma financial statements and accounting, pricing, funding, imputed-cost, float, and cost-recovery policies for priced services.

structure.title: 6 Consumer and Community Affairs

nodes.title: Consumer Compliance Supervision
Consumer Compliance Examinations
key_items: Community Reinvestment Act Performance Evaluation and Regulations
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s consumer and community affairs responsibilities, including examiner training and technology, application analysis, complaint handling, consumer compliance examinations, and enforcement. It reports 2023 examination activity and explains the division of authority with the CFPB, highlights updated HMDA guidance, details CRA examination responsibilities and 2023 ratings, and notes the agencies’ October 2023 CRA final rule. It also introduces fair-lending and UDAP enforcement under ECOA, the Fair Housing Act, and the FTC Act, including ECOA’s prohibited bases of credit discrimination.

nodes.title: Consumer Compliance Enforcement Activities
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 CRA supervision, consumer compliance enforcement, and regulatory modernization activities. It explains the CRA’s community-credit requirements, the Federal Reserve’s examination and outreach roles, the results of 174 state member bank examinations, and the agencies’ October 2023 CRA final rule. It then outlines enforcement of ECOA, the FHA, and the FTC Act, including prohibited discrimination and unfair or deceptive practices, agency responsibilities by bank asset size, investigative and corrective procedures, the referral of one marital-status discrimination matter to the DOJ, and compliance outreach and publications. Finally, it explains flood-insurance requirements under the National Flood Insurance Act and Regulation H and reports a 2023 enforcement order imposing approximately $2.95 million in penalties for flood-insurance violations and unsafe compliance practices.

nodes.title: Mergers and Acquisitions
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve requirements and practices for reviewing mergers and acquisitions, including consideration of competition, financial condition, management and compliance, community needs and CRA performance, and financial stability. Reviews draw on compliance and fair-lending records, supervisory assessments, examiner views, and public or applicant information, with possible pre-membership examinations. The Board publicly reports transaction decisions through press releases, Orders, and semiannual statistics on application outcomes, processing times, withdrawals, and public comments. It also discusses 2023 supervisory coordination with the CFPB and other regulators under an interagency agreement intended to promote cooperation, share examination schedules, and prevent unnecessary burden, duplication, or conflicting supervision, with footnotes linking to relevant guidance and reports.

nodes.title: Coordination with Other Agencies
key_items: Coordination with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
nodes.summary: The text explains the factors and supervisory information the Federal Reserve considers when reviewing mergers and acquisitions, including compliance, fair lending, CRA performance, financial and managerial condition, community needs, competition, and financial stability. It describes possible pre-membership examinations, public disclosure through Board Orders and press releases, and semiannual reporting on application outcomes, processing times, withdrawals, and public comments. It also discusses 2023 coordination between the Federal Reserve and CFPB, together with the OCC, FDIC, and NCUA, to coordinate supervision, share examination schedules, and minimize regulatory burden, duplication, and conflicting directives. Footnotes reference 2015 pre-membership examination guidance and sources for Board Orders and semiannual reports.

nodes.title: Box 6.1. Supporting Consumer Protection and Community Development
Modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve's 2023 consumer-protection and community-development work amid post-pandemic benefit changes, inflation, and banking-sector innovation. It describes DCCA's regulatory, research, and outreach efforts; the joint modernization of CRA regulations; fair-lending and consumer-risk-management initiatives addressing discrimination, algorithmic bias, redlining, and compliance violations; and research on household economic well-being through the SHED survey and related outreach. It also identifies supporting online resources.

nodes.title: Promoting Sound Consumer Risk-Management Practices among Banks
nodes.summary: Box 6.1 of the Federal Reserve’s 2023 Annual Report describes efforts to support consumer protection and community development amid post-pandemic policy changes, inflation, and evolving banking technology. It covers DCCA’s regulatory, research, policy, and outreach work; the joint 2023 modernization of CRA regulations to improve community credit access and reflect modern banking; fair-lending education and consumer-compliance risk management, including disability discrimination, algorithmic bias, redlining, and appraisal discrimination; and research on household financial well-being through the 2022 SHED survey and related outreach. It also references supporting online resources.

nodes.title: Conducting Research and Analysis of Emerging Consumer Issues
nodes.summary: The section describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer-protection and community-development work amid inflation, the end of pandemic benefits, and technological change in banking. It covers DCCA’s regulatory, research, policy, and outreach efforts; the joint modernization of CRA regulations; fair-lending and consumer-compliance risk-management initiatives; and research on household economic well-being through the SHED survey and related outreach. It also references supporting online resources.

nodes.title: Box 6.1—continued
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve research and publications on consumer credit, financial well-being, debt, food-assistance reductions, income, and workforce participation; outreach efforts addressing post-pandemic economic conditions, small-business credit, housing affordability, and low- and moderate-income communities; and housing-focused research seminars. It also explains coordination with other federal banking agencies through shared supervisory practices, interagency guidance, FFIEC examination standards, and participation in the Joint Task Force on Fair Lending, with source notes and links provided.

nodes.title: Engaging with Consumer and Community Perspectives
key_items: Coordination with Other Federal Banking Agencies
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer and community affairs work, including research and publications on credit access, financial well-being, debt, hardship, income, workforce participation, and auto finance; outreach on post-pandemic economic, housing, and community conditions; coordination with federal banking and fair-lending agencies; interagency actions concerning HMDA reporting, LIBOR transition, and CRA modernization; public compliance outreach through publications and webinars; and examiner training designed to build consumer compliance expertise.

nodes.title: Outreach
nodes.summary: The text reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer compliance activities, including interagency efforts on appraisal bias, HMDA reporting relief, LIBOR transition, and CRA modernization. It describes expanded outreach through compliance publications and a fair-lending webinar, and explains the examiner training program’s role in developing supervisory expertise, with supporting online references.

nodes.title: Examiner Training
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer-compliance and community-affairs activities, including interagency work on appraisal bias, HMDA reporting enforcement flexibility, LIBOR transition guidance, and CRA modernization. It outlines public outreach through Consumer Compliance Outlook and an interagency fair-lending webinar; examiner development through commissioning, proficiency testing, and continuing professional education; and 2023 Rapid Response and CPD training offerings. It also explains the Federal Reserve’s role in investigating complaints against its regulated institutions and referring other complaints to the responsible agencies.

nodes.title: Responding to Consumer Complaints and Inquiries
nodes.summary: The text reviews Federal Reserve consumer-compliance examiner commissioning and continuing education, including 2023 examination and professional-development results; explains how the Federal Reserve and Federal Reserve Consumer Help handle consumer complaints and inquiries; reports 2023 complaint volumes, contact methods, product categories, discrimination allegations, and investigation outcomes; describes the Board’s consumer-law regulatory and guidance responsibilities; and details 2024 inflation-indexed thresholds for Regulation Z and Regulation M transaction exemptions and for higher-priced mortgage loan appraisal exemptions.

This section presents the Federal Reserve’s 2023 work supporting consumer protection and community development during post-pandemic economic and technological changes. It covers DCCA’s regulation, research, supervision, outreach, and household-finance analysis; CRA modernization; fair-lending and consumer-risk initiatives; interagency coordination on appraisal bias, HMDA, LIBOR, and fair lending; research and outreach on credit, debt, hardship, housing, small businesses, and low- and moderate-income communities; compliance publications and webinars; examiner commissioning and training; complaint and inquiry handling; the Board’s regulatory responsibilities; and 2024 inflation-indexed consumer-credit and mortgage-appraisal thresholds, with related resources and source links.

The section describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer and community affairs program, centered on consumer protection, fair lending, financial inclusion, community development, and transparent financial markets. It covers supervision and examinations of state member banks and bank holding companies for compliance with major consumer laws and the CRA; examiner training, technology, applications, complaints, HMDA guidance, CRA ratings, and 174 examinations; enforcement of discrimination, UDAP, and flood-insurance requirements; and coordination with the CFPB and other regulators. It also explains CRA modernization and the October 2023 interagency final rule, merger and acquisition review criteria and public reporting, interagency supervisory coordination, and broader research, outreach, stakeholder engagement, publications, training, household-finance analysis, and 2024 regulatory thresholds supporting consumers and communities.

nodes.title: Consumer Laws and Regulations
key_items: Updating Annual Indexes for Consumer Regulations
Annual Indexing of Exempt Consumer Credit and Lease Transactions
Annual Indexing of Threshold for Small Loan Exemption from Appraisal Requirements for Higher-Priced Mortgage Loans
Annual Adjustment to Community Reinvestment Act Asset-Size Thresholds for Small and Intermediate Small Banks
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023 consumer discrimination complaint categories and outcomes, including investigation findings and dispositions. It describes the Board’s consumer-protection and fair-lending regulatory duties, including coordination with the CFPB, and details 2024 CPI-W-based increases to Regulation Z and Regulation M transaction exemptions, the higher-priced mortgage loan appraisal exemption, and CRA small- and intermediate-bank asset thresholds. It also notes the related CRA examination rules and the Board’s continuing research into emerging consumer financial-services issues.

nodes.title: Consumer Research and Analysis of Emerging Issues and Policy
Researching Issues Affecting Consumers and Communities
nodes.summary: In 2023, the Board researched consumer finances and community economic development through surveys, expert discussions, and scholarly work, with an emphasis on emerging issues and post-pandemic recovery. Its 2022 SHED, reported in May 2023, surveyed over 11,000 adults on employment, inflation, income, savings, credit, housing, education, and retirement, documenting worsened financial well-being, greater credit-card debt, reduced spending margins, and declining retirement confidence amid high inflation, along with persistent demographic and income disparities. New questions examined responses to rising prices, financial buffers, worker autonomy, cryptocurrencies, and Buy Now, Pay Later products. Division researchers produced numerous working papers and journal publications on related consumer and community issues. The Federal Reserve’s community development seminar series also continued with a focus on housing-market opportunities for low- and moderate-income households and communities.

nodes.title: Community Development Research Seminar Series
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2022 survey findings and new topics concerning higher prices, financial resilience, worker autonomy, and emerging financial products, noting persistent financial disparities by education, race and ethnicity, and income. It reports substantial 2023 consumer-affairs research output, including working papers, journal publications, and studies on financial well-being, housing, education, public benefits, employment, and lending. It describes the Community Development Research Seminar Series focused on housing-market opportunity, its cross-sector participation and keynote speakers, and Board analysis of emerging consumer risks related to the pandemic, inflation, housing, small-business credit, and new financial products. It also outlines the Federal Reserve’s decentralized community development structure, with Reserve Banks addressing district needs and Board staff coordinating System priorities.

nodes.title: Analysis of Emerging Issues
nodes.summary: The text describes Federal Reserve seminars and emerging-issue analysis, including 2023 research on pandemic-related risks, inflation, housing, and small-business credit; a multi-agency workshop on new consumer financial products; and publications on small-dollar credit and auto finance. It also explains the Federal Reserve’s decentralized community development function, which promotes economic growth and financial stability for underserved communities through research and outreach, with Reserve Bank officers addressing local needs and Board staff coordinating systemwide objectives.

In 2023, the Federal Reserve studied consumer finances, community development, and emerging financial risks through household surveys, research, publications, seminars, expert discussions, and interagency collaboration. Findings from the SHED documented deteriorating financial conditions and persistent demographic and income disparities amid inflation, while new work examined financial resilience, worker autonomy, housing, employment, education, public benefits, lending, small-dollar credit, auto finance, cryptocurrency, and Buy Now, Pay Later products. The Community Development Research Seminar Series focused on housing opportunities for low- and moderate-income communities, and the Federal Reserve’s decentralized community development structure combined local Reserve Bank efforts with Board-level coordination.

nodes.title: Community Development
key_items: Understanding Outcomes in the Labor Market
nodes.summary: The text describes the Federal Reserve’s 2023 work on emerging consumer risks and community development. It covers seminars and expert engagement, analysis of pandemic, inflation, housing, and small-business credit issues, a workshop on new financial products, and publications on small-dollar credit and auto finance. It explains the decentralized community development structure across the 12 Reserve Banks and Board oversight, emphasizing the use of community perspectives in policy and research. It also summarizes research on women’s labor-force participation, workforce conditions, and the post-pandemic health of minority depository institutions, including the MDI annual report and Community Advisory Council observations about rising small-business loan demand and local economic conditions.

structure.summary: The section reviews the Federal Reserve’s 2023 consumer and community affairs activities, including consumer protection, fair-lending and CRA supervision, examinations, complaints, enforcement, regulatory coordination, CRA modernization, merger reviews, and 2024 regulatory thresholds. It also covers research and outreach on household finances, disparities, financial resilience, emerging products and risks, housing, employment, lending, and community development; findings from the SHED and other studies; seminars, publications, and stakeholder engagement; and the decentralized community development framework, including work involving minority depository institutions, women’s labor-force participation, small businesses, and local economic conditions.

structure.title: A Federal Reserve System Organization

nodes.title: Model Validation Council
nodes.summary:
116 110th Annual Report | 2023
Model Validation Council
The Model Validation Council was established in 2012 by the Board of Governors to provide expert and independent advice on its process to rigorously assess the models used in stress tests of banking institutions. The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act required the Federal Reserve to conduct annual stress tests of large bank holding companies and systemically important, nonbank financial institutions supervised by the Board. The Model Validation Council provides input on the Board’s efforts to assess the effectiveness of the models used in the stress tests. The council is intended to improve the quality of the Federal Reserve’s model assessment program and to strengthen the confidence in the integrity and independence of the program.
Members
The council had no members or meetings during 2023.

nodes.title: Rules and Regulations
nodes.summary: This excerpt introduces the Board of Governors’ 2023 record of policy actions and explains its statutory basis, action categories, voting disclosures, source materials, and separation of FOMC actions. It summarizes rules on insurance-related capital requirements, Community Reinvestment Act modernization, and administrative procedures, followed by policy statements updating credit-loss accounting guidance, commercial real estate workout and accommodation guidance, and restrictions on state member bank activities under section 9(13), including novel crypto-related activities. It also records effective dates, interagency participation, voting results, later CRA amendments, personnel changes, and Federal Register references.

nodes.title: Policy Statements and Other Actions
Allowances for Credit Losses
nodes.summary: The text records three Board policy actions in 2023: an interagency update removing TDR references from allowances-for-credit-losses guidance following CECL-related accounting changes; updated interagency guidance on commercial real estate loan workouts and short-term accommodations for stressed but creditworthy borrowers; and a policy interpreting Federal Reserve Act section 9(13), generally aligning state member bank activity limits with those for national banks and applying consistent restrictions, including to novel crypto-related activities. It also emphasizes legal compliance, safe and sound operations, risk management, and internal controls, identifies the approving officials, and provides Federal Register citations.

nodes.title: Commercial Real Estate Loan Accommodations and Workouts
nodes.summary: The text records three Board policy actions in 2023: an interagency update removing obsolete TDR references from credit-loss allowance guidance following CECL-related accounting changes; updated interagency guidance on commercial real estate loan workouts and short-term accommodations during borrower stress; and a section 9(13) policy establishing generally uniform activity limits for state member and other Board-supervised banks, including novel crypto-asset activities, while emphasizing legal authorization, safety and soundness, risk management, and internal controls. All actions received unanimous votes from the listed Board members, and Federal Register links are provided.

nodes.title: Policy Statement on Section 9(13) of the Federal Reserve Act
nodes.summary: The text records 2023 Board policy actions on credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate workouts and short-term accommodations, limits on state member bank activities under section 9(13), climate-related financial risk management for large institutions, and emergency measures responding to the SVB and Signature Bank failures. It explains the purpose and scope of each policy, identifies interagency partners and applicable statutory authorities, records voting outcomes—including dissent on the climate-risk principles—and describes the systemic-risk exception recommendation and creation of the Bank Term Funding Program, with cited Federal Register notices and press releases.

nodes.title: Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text covers Board requirements for adequate information systems, approval and voting details for interagency climate-related financial risk-management principles applicable to financial institutions with over $100 billion in assets, and the Board’s March 2023 response to the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank. That response included recommending the systemic risk exception to the FDIC’s least-cost-resolution rule and creating the Bank Term Funding Program under section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, with explanations of the bank failures, financial-stability rationale, statutory authority, Treasury approval requirement, and lending limitations. It also contains related footnote references, with the final discussion truncated.

nodes.title: Systemic Risk Exception and Bank Term Funding Program
nodes.summary: The passage records Board actions and votes on information-system adequacy, climate-related financial risk principles for large institutions, the systemic risk exception and emergency BTFP response to the 2023 bank failures, and interagency third-party risk-management guidance. It explains the purposes, eligibility, collateral, pricing, statutory basis, and later modification and closure of the BTFP, identifies supporting references, and lists all approving and dissenting governors for each action.

nodes.title: Third-Party Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text describes emergency lending requirements and the Board’s creation and later modification and scheduled closure of the BTFP, including eligibility, collateral, maturity, valuation, interest-rate terms, and supporting votes. It also covers the Board’s June 2023 final interagency third-party risk-management guidance with the FDIC and OCC, its purpose and principles, the voting outcome, and related reference links.

nodes.title: Interest on Reserves
nodes.summary: The text records the Federal Reserve Board's 2023 decisions on interest paid on reserve balances: three increases from 4.4% to 5.4% between February and July, followed by maintenance at 5.4% through December, each aligned with corresponding FOMC federal funds target-range decisions and accompanied by voting records. It also explains the statutory process for setting discount-window rates for depository institutions, including biweekly review of primary, secondary, and seasonal credit rates, and refers readers to year-end rate tables, meeting minutes, press releases, and online historical rate data.

This section records the Federal Reserve Board's 2023 policy statements and other actions concerning credit-loss allowances, commercial real estate workouts, Section 9(13) activity limits including crypto-related activities, climate-related financial risk management, emergency measures after the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures, third-party risk management, interest on reserve balances, and discount-window rates. It explains the purposes, legal authorities, scope, operational requirements, risk-management expectations, emergency lending terms, eligibility and collateral rules, later BTFP changes and closure, and statutory rate-setting procedures; identifies interagency partners, approving and dissenting officials, voting outcomes, and Treasury involvement; and provides related Federal Register citations, press releases, meeting materials, footnotes, and historical rate references.

nodes.title: Discount Rates for Depository Institutions in 2023
key_items: Votes on Changes to Discount Rates for Depository Institutions
nodes.summary: The text records the Board's September, November, and December 2023 decisions to keep the interest rate on reserve balances at 5.4% while the FOMC maintained the federal funds target range at 5¼–5½%, including the voting members. It explains the statutory review process for discount-window rates and reports year-end 2023 rates of 5.50% for primary credit, 6.00% for secondary credit, and 5.35% for seasonal credit. It describes the purposes and pricing of the three credit programs, the availability of primary credit for up to 90 days, and the four 2023 increases in the primary credit rate—from 4.5% to 5.5%—with their effective dates, participating Reserve Banks, and Board voting records.

nodes.title: The Board of Governors and the Government Performance and Results Act
key_items: Four-year Strategic Plan, Annual Performance Plan, and Annual Performance Report
nodes.summary: The text explains that, although exempt from GPRA, the Federal Reserve Board voluntarily follows its planning and reporting framework by publishing a multiyear strategic plan, annual performance plan, and annual performance report. It describes the 2020–23 strategic plan’s five functional areas and its focus on prioritized mission objectives with flexibility for emerging challenges; explains that the annual plan organizes yearly initiatives and resources; and notes that the annual report records progress and promotes transparency. These processes support prioritization, execution, and public communication of the Board’s critical work, with the documents available on the Board’s website.

structure.summary: The section documents the Federal Reserve Board’s 2023 policy actions, rules, regulations, policy statements, emergency and financial-risk measures, voting and interagency details, legal authorities, effective dates, and supporting Federal Register and other source materials. It also reports 2023 reserve-balance and discount-window rate decisions and changes, explains the three credit programs and their statutory review process, and describes the Board’s strategic planning, annual performance planning, reporting, and transparency practices under its voluntary use of the GPRA framework.

structure.title: F Litigation
structure.summary: The report states that the Board was involved in 16 litigation matters in 2023—7 new and 9 carried over, matching 2022—and that 11 remained pending at year-end. The pending matters involved master-account challenges, a contract and debt-collection action, Regulation II debit interchange fee litigation, a bank-acquisition review, and FOIA requests. Five matters were resolved through stipulated dismissals, dismissal of an APA claim, or appellate affirmance of the Board’s orders.

structure.title: G Statistical Tables

nodes.title: Table G.1. Federal Reserve open market transactions, 2023 Millions of dollars
nodes.summary: Appendix G presents statistical tables on Federal Reserve operations and holdings. Table G.1 details monthly and annual 2023 open market transactions, including Treasury purchases, sales, exchanges, redemptions, agency obligations, mortgage-backed-security settlements, total holdings changes, and temporary repurchase and reverse repurchase operations, with explanatory methodological notes. Table G.2 gives December 31 holdings of Treasury and federal agency securities for 2021–23, broken down by maturity and type, together with the changes between years.

nodes.title: Table G.2. Federal Reserve Bank holdings of U.S. Treasury and federal agency securities, December 31, 2021–23 Millions of dollars
nodes.summary: The text presents Federal Reserve balance-sheet statistical tables: Table G.2 details 2021–23 holdings of Treasury securities, federal agency securities, and mortgage-backed securities by maturity, type, and issuer, along with repurchase and reverse-repurchase transactions, annual changes, and explanatory valuation and collateral notes. Table G.3 lists the 2023 reserve requirements for three liability categories, all at zero percent, with their effective dates and a note concerning the applicable maintenance period and Regulation D.

nodes.title: Table G.3. Reserve requirements of depository institutions, December 31, 2023
nodes.summary: The text presents two Federal Reserve statistical tables. Table G.3 shows that reserve requirements for net transaction accounts, nonpersonal time deposits, and Eurocurrency liabilities were all 0 percent at year-end 2023, with their applicable effective dates and explanatory notes. Table G.4 compares 2022 and 2023 counts and changes in U.S. banks, branches and additional offices, and banks affiliated with bank holding companies, including detailed classifications for national, state member, state nonmember, and savings banks. It records new institutions or branches, bank-to-branch conversions, ceased or discontinued operations, other changes, net changes, and year-end totals, while also providing definitions, coverage of U.S. territories and possessions, and references to Regulation Y and Regulation D.

nodes.title: Table G.4. Banking offices and banks affiliated with bank holding companies in the United States, December 31, 2022 and 2023
nodes.summary: The excerpt contains two Federal Reserve statistical tables. Table G.4 details changes in U.S. banks, branches and additional offices, and bank-holding-company-affiliated banks between year-end 2022 and 2023, broken down by institution type and banking classification, with definitions and coverage notes. Table G.5A provides year-end 1984–2023 and month-end 2023 amounts in millions of dollars for depository-institution reserves, Federal Reserve credit, reserve-supplying factors, float, Treasury currency and coin, gold stock, special drawing rights, and the Treasury certificate account.

nodes.title: Table G.5A. Reserves of depository institutions, Federal Reserve Bank credit, and related items, year-end 1984–2023 and month-end 2023 Millions of dollars
nodes.summary: The text reproduces Federal Reserve statistical Tables G.5A and G.5B on depository-institution reserves, Federal Reserve credit, and related balance-sheet items. Table G.5A covers year-end 1984–2023 plus monthly 2023 data, organizing sources and uses of reserve funds and documenting the dramatic expansion and subsequent reduction of Federal Reserve credit and the high level of reserve balances. It includes detailed definitions and historical notes for securities, repurchase agreements, lending facilities, Treasury and Federal Reserve accounts, clearing balances, deferred assets, and rounding. Table G.5B extends the historical series back to 1918 and lists the corresponding reserve-supplying categories through 1983.

nodes.title: Table G.5B. Reserves of depository institutions, Federal Reserve Bank credit, and related items, year-end 1918–1983 Millions of dollars
nodes.summary: The text reproduces Federal Reserve Statistical Table G.5B, a detailed 1918–1983 annual series on factors supplying and absorbing reserve funds, including Federal Reserve credit, gold, Treasury currency, deposits, liabilities, member-bank reserves, required reserves, and excess reserves, together with methodological and definitional notes. It then presents Table G.6, comparing the principal assets, liabilities, capital, and bank counts of U.S.-insured commercial banks by total, national and state member banks, and nonmember banks for June 30, 2023 and 2022, with coverage, rounding, and revision notes.

nodes.title: Table G.6. Principal assets and liabilities of insured commercial banks, by class of bank, June 30, 2023 and 2022
nodes.summary: The text contains two statistical tables from the 2023 Annual Report. Table G.6 compares the assets, liabilities, capital, and bank counts of U.S.-insured commercial banks by bank class for June 30, 2023 and 2022, with detailed loan, investment, cash, deposit, and coverage notes. Table G.7 provides the historical percentages and effective dates of initial margin requirements for short sales, margin stocks, and convertible bonds under Regulations T, U, and X, together with explanations of the regulations, their effective dates and evolution, and the meaning of the historical notation.

nodes.title: Table G.7. Initial margin requirements under Regulations T, U, and X
nodes.summary: The excerpt contains a historical table of initial margin requirements under Regulations T, U, and X, including requirements for short sales, margin stocks, and convertible bonds, explanatory regulatory notes, effective dates, and the former Regulation G’s merger into Regulation U. It also begins a Federal Reserve Banks statement-of-condition table for December 31, 2023 and 2022, listing systemwide and individual-bank asset categories and amounts in millions of dollars. Systemwide loans and securities and total assets decreased substantially in 2023, and detailed figures are shown for Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, and Richmond before the table continues.

nodes.title: Table G.8A. Statement of condition of the Federal Reserve Banks, by Bank, December 31, 2023 and 2022 Millions of dollars
nodes.summary: The text reproduces Federal Reserve statistical Tables G.8A and G.8B. Table G.8A gives comparative 2023 and 2022 balance sheets for the Federal Reserve System and each of its 12 Reserve Banks, covering detailed assets, liabilities, capital accounts, consolidated-entity interests, and total balances. Explanatory notes define accounting, valuation, consolidation, deposit, remittance, and rounding treatments, as well as notation. Table G.8B reconciles Federal Reserve notes outstanding and notes not subject to collateralization with collateral held in gold certificates, special drawing rights certificates, and U.S. Treasury securities, including a face-value clarification for Treasury securities.

nodes.title: Table G.8B. Statement of condition of the Federal Reserve Banks, December 31, 2023 and 2022 Millions of dollars
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents Federal Reserve financial statistics. Table G.8B compares note liabilities and their collateral at year-end 2023 and 2022, showing increased notes outstanding and collateralized notes in 2023, with collateral primarily consisting of Treasury securities plus gold and special drawing rights certificates. Table G.9, continued from the 2023 Annual Report, provides systemwide and individual Federal Reserve Bank income, expense, net-income, and investment-sale adjustment data for Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, and Richmond, covering lending and investment interest income, other income, operating and financial expenses, pension and reimbursable costs, and gains or losses on securities sales.

nodes.title: Table G.9. Income and expenses of the Federal Reserve Banks, by Bank, 2023 Thousands of dollars
nodes.summary: The excerpt contains Federal Reserve Annual Report Tables G.9 and G.10. Table G.9 gives detailed 2023 income, expenses, gains and losses, comprehensive income, Treasury remittances, and distributions for the system total and each of the 12 Reserve Banks, including explanations of the accounting and assessment footnotes. Table G.10 begins a long-run 1914–2023 historical series for all Banks, showing income, expenses, assessments, deductions, surplus and comprehensive-income transfers, dividends, statutory-reserve transfers, Federal Reserve note interest, and Treasury distributions; the visible data run through 1949 and continue in the original table.

nodes.title: Table G.10. Income and expenses of the Federal Reserve Banks, 1914–2023 Thousands of dollars
nodes.summary: The text presents two Federal Reserve statistical tables. Table G.10 gives annual all-bank financial data for 1914–2023 and cumulative totals by Reserve Bank, covering income, expenses, assessments, operational costs, dividends, Treasury distributions, Federal Reserve note interest, surplus transfers, and comprehensive income, with explanatory statutory and accounting notes. Table G.11 gives 2020–23 volumes and dollar values for major Reserve Bank processing and payment operations, including currency, coin, checks, securities, funds, and automated clearinghouse transactions, together with definitions and revision notes.

nodes.title: Table G.11. Operations in principal departments of the Federal Reserve Banks, 2020–23
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents two statistical tables from the Federal Reserve’s 2023 Annual Report. Table G.11 gives 2020–23 volumes and dollar values for major Reserve Bank payment, currency, coin, check, securities-transfer, funds-transfer, and ACH operations, with notes on electronic checks, excluded transactions, and revised data. Table G.12 gives December 31, 2023 officer and employee counts and annual salaries for each Reserve Bank and Federal Reserve Information Technology, including presidents, other officers, full-time staff, part-time staff, temporary/hourly workers, and totals, followed by definitions and organizational notes.

nodes.title: Table G.12. Number and annual salaries of officers and employees of the Federal Reserve Banks, December 31, 2023
nodes.summary: The text contains two Federal Reserve statistical tables for December 31, 2023. Table G.12 details presidents, other officers, and employees of the Reserve Banks and Federal Reserve Information Technology by headcount and annual salary, including aggregate totals and explanatory notes on rounding, salary definitions, temporary staff, Atlanta's benefits-office change, and the St. Louis presidency. Table G.13 presents acquisition costs and net book values for land, buildings, premises, and other real estate at Reserve Bank and branch locations, with aggregate dollar totals, not-applicable entries, and notes on pending construction-account allocations and the consolidation of Phoenix costs into the Los Angeles Branch.

nodes.title: Table G.13. Acquisition costs and net book value of the premises of the Federal Reserve Banks and Branches, December 31, 2023
nodes.summary: Table G.13 reports, in thousands of dollars, the December 31, 2023 land, building, and total acquisition costs and net book values of Federal Reserve premises across all listed Banks and Branches. Totals are $445,458 thousand for land, $3,488,630 thousand for buildings, $3,934,088 thousand for acquisition costs, and $1,939,828 thousand for net book value. Other real estate is $94,771 thousand for Boston and not applicable elsewhere. Notes explain the treatment of pending construction expenditures and the consolidation of Phoenix costs into Los Angeles, followed by Federal Reserve publication and website information.

structure.summary: Appendix G compiles Federal Reserve statistical tables covering open market operations; securities holdings; reserve requirements; U.S. banking offices and affiliated banks; historical and current reserve, Federal Reserve credit, and balance-sheet data; insured commercial-bank finances; margin regulations; Federal Reserve Bank statements of condition, note collateral, income, expenses, distributions, and long-run financial history; payment and processing operations; personnel and salaries; and Reserve Bank premises costs and values. The tables include systemwide, individual-Bank, institutional, maturity, issuer, and historical breakdowns, along with definitions, accounting, valuation, collateral, regulatory, coverage, revision, rounding, and organizational notes.
